doc.title: Wayne Bergeron interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 29, 2020

title: Using tuners with eyes closed
summary: Bergeron explains how he teaches players to use a tuner as a tool without relying on their eyes.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Yeah. If you take your eyes out of the equation, the other senses take over you know. So I feel the same way about, on the technical side. Because I’m a big promoter of tuners, using digital tuners, for a learning tool. And I have some that I clip on my bell because like sometimes I’m in a situation where I can’t hear the bass and I want to have some reference of where I’m at. But if you use a tuner and you just stare at it all the time, you stop listening with your ears and you start listening with your eyes. You know? And so what I suggest with tuners for players, I said, “Tuners are great and I think they’re as valuable as a metronome. But you wouldn’t bring a metronome to a gig and then say ‘hey they’re rushing or dragging,’ you’ll be flexible of course.” You know. But with the tuner what I’ll do is I shut my eyes and I hit a note, and I bend the note up and down and I try to find the bull’s eye of the note, where it’s resonant. And then I’ll open my eyes and I’ll look at the tuner. And I’ll go okay, there, that’s right in tune there, and that’s where the sound is most resonant. Funny how that works you know.

Or, it can also tell you where you need to put your slide, your tuning slide. Because if you shut your eyes and you’re in the most resonant place and you open your eyes and it’s reading sharp, well then you’re not playing down the middle of the instrument — you’re playing down the middle of the instrument but the instrument is too short. You have to lengthen it a little bit.

Because to really be in tune now you’re blipping the notes. And so that creates another — so that’s a little something I’ve learned from using those. And I know players that try to stare at them, a couple of French horn players I’d worked with in the pit are really self- conscious about their pitch because in the pit it sounds like hell and it’s hard to hear and it makes you very not confident about where you’re putting your note. Your French horn might be behind us and you can’t hear us. So he would use a tuner all the time, this guy. And I’d hear, like we’d hit a chord and it’d be perfectly in tune, and then I’d hear him bending his note down because it says he’s sharp. But he maybe has the minor third or something you know. And he needs to be bringing it up. You know. So stuff like that can
happen. I think the tuner is a really important tool in our practice, though, if used in the right way anyway.
